items.pronunciation_notes: रूप has a long uu and the final vowel drops: do ruup, two syllables.
items.gloss_en: the two forms every noun has

learn.explanation_en: Every Hindi noun has two forms. The one you learned in Module 4 is the direct form, used when the noun is the subject or stands alone. The second is the oblique form, used whenever a postposition follows. बेटा is the direct form; बेटे को is the oblique. For some nouns the two look identical, which is why Module 5 could avoid the whole question — every noun it used was one of those.

examples.note: The direct form, as learned in Module 4.
The oblique form, because a postposition follows.
घर looks the same in both forms, which is why Module 5 used it constantly.

common_error.why_en: A postposition forces the oblique form, and बेटा changes to बेटे.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: बेटा + को
practice.explanation_en: One son, and a postposition follows, so बेटा becomes बेटे.

game.explanation_en: बेटा को is wrong — a postposition requires the oblique बेटे. The others are all correct.

items.pronunciation_notes: The vowel after र drops, giving parsarg in two syllables.
items.gloss_en: the postposition — what triggers the change

learn.explanation_en: Only one thing forces the oblique form: a postposition following the noun. में, पर, से, को, तक, का and the compounds built on के all do it. Nothing else does — not being an object, not being plural, not being anywhere in particular. If there is no postposition after the noun, the noun stays in its direct form. That single rule is the whole trigger, and it is worth over-learning.

examples.note: No postposition, so the direct form stays.
को follows, so the noun goes oblique.
A compound postposition triggers it exactly the same way.

common_error.why_en: There is no postposition here, so the noun stays in its direct form.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: बच्चा + के लिए
practice.explanation_en: के लिए is a postposition, so बच्चा becomes बच्चे.

game.explanation_en: बच्चे अच्छा है is wrong — with no postposition the noun should stay बच्चा.

items.pronunciation_notes: तिरछा has an aspirated छ, and the vowel after त drops: tirchhaa.

learn.explanation_en: Not every noun looks different in the oblique. घर is घर in both, and so are किताब, चाय and शहर — which is exactly why Module 5 could build sentences with postpositions and never mention any of this. But बेटा becomes बेटे, and in the plural almost every noun changes. Hindi nouns fall into six classes by how they behave, and this module works through them one at a time.

examples.note: No change at all — the direct and oblique forms are identical.
Also unchanged.
कमरा changes to कमरे, because it ends in -ा.

common_error.why_en: कमरा ends in -ा, so it changes before a postposition — unlike घर, which does not.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: कमरा + में
practice.explanation_en: कमरा ends in -ा and is singular, so the oblique is कमरे.

game.explanation_en: कमरा में is wrong. घर and किताब do not change, but कमरा must become कमरे.

summary.recap_en: This level introduced the central fact of the module: every noun has a direct form and an oblique form, and a postposition is the only thing that triggers the switch. Some nouns look identical in both, which is why Module 5 could ignore the whole question.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the first noun class — masculines ending in -ा, which change the most visibly.

items.pronunciation_notes: बेटे ends in a flat ए with no glide, and को is unstressed: beṭe ko.

learn.explanation_en: Masculine nouns ending in -ा are the first class, and they are the most visible: the -ा becomes -े before any postposition. बेटा को is never right; बेटे को is. This class includes a great many everyday words — बच्चा, कुत्ता, कमरा, दरवाज़ा, जूता, कपड़ा — so once you can spot the -ा ending you have a rule that pays off constantly.

examples.note: The -ा becomes -े before को.
Any postposition does it, compound ones included.
And से as well.

common_error.why_en: A masculine noun in -ा must change to -े before a postposition.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: बेटा + से
practice.explanation_en: One son, so the -ा becomes -े and gives बेटे.

game.explanation_en: बेटा को keeps the direct form where the oblique बेटे is required.

items.pronunciation_notes: The च्च stack holds the ch with no breath on either half: bachche se.

learn.explanation_en: The rule does not depend on the word. Any masculine noun ending in -ा behaves identically: बच्चा becomes बच्चे, कुत्ता becomes कुत्ते, दरवाज़ा becomes दरवाज़े. There are no exceptions inside this class, which makes it the easiest of the six to learn — the difficulty is only in remembering to apply it while you are speaking.

examples.note: बच्चा becomes बच्चे.
कुत्ता behaves the same way.
And so does दरवाज़ा.

common_error.why_en: कुत्ता ends in -ा, so it takes the oblique कुत्ते before a postposition.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: दरवाज़ा + पर
practice.explanation_en: One door, and a postposition follows, so दरवाज़ा becomes दरवाज़े.

game.explanation_en: कुत्ता को should be कुत्ते को. The other three have all made the change correctly.

items.pronunciation_notes: The vowel after क drops, so कमरे is two syllables: kam-re.

learn.title_en: In the room, not in the कमरा
learn.explanation_en: Location postpositions trigger the oblique just as को and से do. कमरे में, दरवाज़े पर, घोड़े पर — all of them take the changed form. This matters because location phrases are among the first things a learner wants to say, and कमरा में is one of the most audible mistakes there is. Say कमरे में a dozen times and the habit sticks.

examples.note: कमरा becomes कमरे before में.
घोड़ा behaves identically.

examples.english: There is a table in the room.
examples.note: A full sentence, and the verb still comes last.

common_error.why_en: में is a postposition, so कमरा must take its oblique form कमरे.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: घोड़ा + पर
practice.explanation_en: One horse, so घोड़ा becomes घोड़े.

game.explanation_en: कमरा में is wrong. घर needs no change, but कमरा does.

summary.recap_en: This level covered Class 1 in the singular: masculine nouns ending in -ा change that -ा to -े before any postposition, with no exceptions inside the class.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the same class in the plural, where the ending changes again.

items.pronunciation_notes: The dot nasalises the ओ, so बेटों ends in a hum: beṭoṁ.

learn.explanation_en: In the plural, Class 1 nouns take -ों before a postposition: बेटे becomes बेटों, बच्चे becomes बच्चों. This -ों ending is not confined to Class 1 — nearly every Hindi noun takes it in the plural oblique, whatever class it belongs to. That makes it the single most useful ending in the module, and the one to learn first.

examples.note: Plural and oblique, so -ों.
The same ending with a compound postposition.
And again with से.

common_error.why_en: For more than one son the plural oblique बेटों is needed, not the singular oblique बेटे.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: बच्चे + के लिए
practice.explanation_en: More than one child, and a postposition follows, so the form is बच्चों.

game.explanation_en: कुत्ताओं से adds an ending to the direct form instead of replacing it. The plural oblique is कुत्तों.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both words end in a nasalised vowel, so the phrase hums twice: kamroṁ meṁ.
items.gloss_en: Class 1 plural with a location postposition

learn.explanation_en: The plural oblique works the same way with location postpositions. कमरों में, दरवाज़ों पर, घोड़ों पर. Notice the shape of the whole system for this class: three forms, and each has one job. कमरा stands alone, कमरे is either the plain plural or the singular before a postposition, and कमरों is the plural before a postposition.

examples.note: Plural and oblique together.
The same ending with पर.

examples.english: There are tables in the rooms.
examples.note: A full sentence, with the verb last as always.

common_error.why_en: If more than one room is meant, the noun needs the plural oblique कमरों.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: दरवाज़े + पर
practice.explanation_en: More than one door, and पर follows, so the form is दरवाज़ों.

game.explanation_en: कमराओं में is not a Hindi form. The -ा is replaced by -ों, not added to.

items.pronunciation_notes: The three differ only in their final vowel, and the third adds a nasal hum.

learn.title_en: Three forms, and what each is for
learn.explanation_en: A Class 1 noun has three shapes and each does a clear job. बेटा is the direct singular: one son, no postposition. बेटे is either the direct plural or the oblique singular — it covers both, which is a genuine ambiguity you have to read around. बेटों is the oblique plural. Learn the three as a set and the class is finished.

examples.note: Direct singular — no postposition anywhere.
Direct plural, and the verb confirms it.
Oblique plural, because को follows.

common_error.why_en: There is no postposition here, so the plural stays in its direct form बेटे.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: बेटे + को
practice.explanation_en: Plural and followed by a postposition, so the form is बेटों.

game.explanation_en: बेटों अच्छे हैं has an oblique form with no postposition to justify it. It should be बेटे.

summary.recap_en: This level completed Class 1. Three forms: बेटा alone, बेटे for the plain plural or the singular before a postposition, and बेटों for the plural before a postposition. The -ों ending will return in every class that follows.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the ambiguity of the middle form, and a drill on where it goes wrong.

items.pronunciation_notes: A flat ए with no glide, and identical whichever of its two jobs it is doing.

learn.explanation_en: बेटे is the direct plural and also the oblique singular, and nothing in the word tells you which. What tells you is what comes next. If a postposition follows, it is one son in the oblique. If no postposition follows, it is several sons in the direct form. बेटे को is to one son; बेटे अच्छे हैं is several sons are good. Reading Hindi means checking the next word before deciding.

examples.note: को follows, so this is one son in the oblique.
No postposition, so this is several sons.

examples.english: There is a table in the room.
examples.note: One room, oblique, because में follows.

common_error.why_en: The verb agrees with चाय, which is singular. बेटे here is one son, not several.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its singular oblique form.
practice.question: कमरा + में
practice.explanation_en: One room and a postposition following, so the form is कमरे.

game.explanation_en: बेटे अच्छा है mixes a plural noun with a singular adjective and verb. With no postposition, बेटे must be plural throughout.

items.pronunciation_notes: The only audible difference is the nasal hum on the second, which is easy to lose in fast speech.
items.gloss_en: one against many in the oblique

learn.explanation_en: Once a postposition is in place, the only thing separating one from many is the ending: कुत्ते को for one dog, कुत्तों को for several. Nothing else in the phrase changes, and in speech the difference is a single nasal hum. This is where careless listening costs you meaning, and where the -ों ending earns its keep.

examples.note: One dog.
Several, marked only by the -ों.

examples.english: There is tea for the children.
examples.note: Plural oblique inside a full sentence.

common_error.why_en: If several dogs are meant, the plural oblique कुत्तों is required — the singular form does not cover both.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: कुत्ते + को
practice.explanation_en: Several dogs before a postposition, so the form is कुत्तों.

game.explanation_en: कुत्ता को uses the direct form before a postposition. Both कुत्ते को and कुत्तों को are correct, for one dog and several.

items.pronunciation_notes: Four words, with the oblique कमरे and the postposition में running together in speech.

learn.explanation_en: The oblique form changes the noun and nothing else. The verb still agrees with whatever the subject is, the word order is unchanged, and the postposition still follows its noun. कमरे में मेज़ है has an oblique noun at the front and a verb agreeing with मेज़ at the back, and the two have nothing to do with each other. Keeping them separate in your head is the whole trick.

examples.english: There is a table in the room.
examples.note: Oblique noun, and the verb agrees with मेज़.

examples.english: There are tables in the rooms.
examples.note: Both are plural now, but independently.

examples.english: There is milk for the children.
examples.note: Plural oblique, and a singular verb agreeing with दूध.

common_error.why_en: The verb agrees with दूध, which is singular. The plural oblique noun has no effect on it.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: कमरे + में
practice.explanation_en: More than one room before a postposition gives कमरों.

game.explanation_en: The verb must agree with दूध, which is singular. A plural oblique noun earlier in the sentence changes nothing.

summary.recap_en: This level drilled the ambiguity at the centre of Class 1. बेटे is both the plain plural and the oblique singular, and only the next word tells you which — while the verb goes on agreeing with the subject regardless.
summary.next_up_en: Next: Class 2, the masculines that do not change in the singular at all.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two short words that run together in speech, with the nasal hum closing the phrase.
items.gloss_en: Class 2 singular — no change at all

learn.explanation_en: Class 2 is every masculine noun that does not end in -ा: घर, शहर, गाँव, बाज़ार, स्कूल, दिन. In the singular these do not change at all before a postposition — घर is घर whether it stands alone or has में after it. This is the class Module 5 leaned on for every one of its examples, which is why postpositions felt so easy there.

examples.note: No change from the direct form.
Also unchanged.
And again — nothing happens.

common_error.why_en: घर does not end in -ा, so there is no -े form for it to take.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its oblique form.
practice.question: शहर + में
practice.explanation_en: One city, and Class 2 nouns do not change in the singular, so शहर stays as it is.

game.explanation_en: घरे में invents an ending. Class 2 nouns take no ending at all in the singular oblique.

items.pronunciation_notes: Both words end in a nasalised vowel: gharoṁ meṁ, with two hums in a row.

learn.explanation_en: Class 2 does nothing in the singular, but the plural oblique is another matter: घर becomes घरों, शहर becomes शहरों. This is the same -ों you met in Class 1, and it will keep returning — it is the one ending shared by almost every class in the module. So the rule for Class 2 is short: nothing in the singular, -ों in the plural.

examples.note: The plural oblique takes -ों.
The same ending, and the middle vowel drops in speech.

examples.english: There are people in the houses.
examples.note: A full sentence with the plural oblique at the front.

common_error.why_en: If more than one house is meant, the plural oblique घरों is needed — the unchanged form covers only the singular.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: शहर + में
practice.explanation_en: More than one city before a postposition, so the form is शहरों.

game.explanation_en: घरें में uses a feminine plural ending on a masculine noun. The plural oblique is घरों.

items.pronunciation_notes: The vowel after श drops and the ending hums, giving shahroṁ in two syllables.
items.gloss_en: Class 2 singular and plural side by side
items.setting_en: Two people comparing city and village life

learn.explanation_en: Listen for the difference between शहर में and शहरों में in the exchange below. One city takes no ending at all; several take -ों. The two are only a hum apart, and since Class 2 covers a large share of the place names you will need, this is a contrast worth being able to hear rather than only to read.

lines.speaker: A
lines.hindi: क्या यह घर शहर में है?
lines.read_as: kyaa yah ghar shahar meṁ hai?
lines.english: Is this house in the city?

lines.speaker: B
lines.english: No, it is in the village.

lines.speaker: B
lines.hindi: हाँ, लेकिन गाँवों में सस्ते हैं।
lines.read_as: hãa, lekin gãavoṁ meṁ saste haiṁ.
lines.english: Yes, but in villages they are cheap.

common_error.why_en: The claim is about cities in general, so the plural oblique शहरों is needed.

practice.prompt_en: Put this noun into its plural oblique form.
practice.question: गाँव + में
practice.explanation_en: More than one village before a postposition, so the form is गाँवों.

game.question_en: Listen to the third line. Which word is missing?
game.mask_reason: the plural oblique form of a Class 2 noun
game.explanation_en: The statement is about cities in general and में follows, so the plural oblique शहरों is required.

tts_strings: क्या यह घर शहर में है?
हाँ, लेकिन गाँवों में सस्ते हैं।

summary.recap_en: This level opened Class 2: masculine nouns that do not end in -ा. They do not change at all in the singular, which is why Module 5 could use them freely, but the plural oblique still takes -ों.
summary.next_up_en: Next: more of Class 2, and then the masculines ending in -ी.
